name: Nidaros Cathedral
label: Nidaros Cathedral
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/417245741: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Nidaros Cathedral' (114 m across).
notes: Norway's national cathedral, best photographed from the square in front of its ornate west front.

text.description:
Nidaros Cathedral is the cathedral in the city of Trondheim, and it is the top-ranked spot on this Trondheim map. It stands over the burial place of King Olav II, who died in 1030 and became Norway's patron saint. Building began in 1070 and the cathedral was substantially complete around 1300. Fires and rebuilding followed, and the major restoration that began in 1869 was officially completed in 2001. It is described as the northernmost medieval cathedral in the world, and its style mixes Romanesque and Gothic. It is still a working church that seats about 1,850 people, and Norwegian monarchs are still consecrated here.

It photographs well because of its sheer size and its many pointed, layered stonework shapes. Stand square-on, let the cathedral fill the middle of the picture, and leave a little sky above the roofline. Then step closer for a second shot of the stonework and carved detail. If people are passing, wait a moment for a clearer view. It is a place of worship, so be discreet when taking photos near visitors.
text.geographic_location: Nidaros Cathedral is in the city of Trondheim, in Trøndelag county.
text.directions_text: No stations or tram stops are listed for this spot, so head for the cathedral on foot or use a local navigation app on your phone. The phone icon on the map is about 55 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from where you stand for the whole building. If the cathedral does not quite fit, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x), and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for towers, windows and stone details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 55 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. From here the whole building fits in one frame without you having to stand right up against the walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the cathedral up with the vertical lines so the walls do not lean. Keep the building central, with some sky above it. Take a wide shot first, then a telephoto shot of the stonework and details. If you move closer, hold the phone level to avoid distorted edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the cathedral to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its detail. Try a panorama only if you can hold the phone steady and nobody is walking across the scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or early evening is a good time to try, as the light is usually softer then. In the evening, use night mode and hold the phone steady against something solid.

text.access_note: The cathedral is a working place of worship and may have ticketed areas or visiting restrictions, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Standing 104 m west of the cathedral means you look east towards it, so afternoon and evening sun is usually behind you or to the side.
Late afternoon or early evening light is usually softer than midday light.
The stand-here point is outdoors in open public space, from which the cathedral can be photographed from outside.
Visitors may be walking around the cathedral and may appear in photos.

name: Archbishop's Palace
label: Archbishop's Palace
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/538808455: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Erkebispegården' (146 m across).
notes: Medieval palace beside the cathedral, one of Scandinavia's oldest secular buildings.

text.description:
The Archbishop's Palace (Erkebispegården) is a big stone complex that for centuries was the seat and home of the Archbishop of Nidaros. It is one of the largest medieval stone buildings in Scandinavia, and its oldest walls are probably from the 13th century. That age shows in the heavy masonry, which gives you plenty of texture and character to photograph.

After the Reformation it became royal property. It was later rebuilt as a residential palace and then used more for military purposes. Today it houses several museums, is regularly used by the Church of Norway, and hosts the Olavsfestdagene festival. The Regalia of Norway have been on permanent display in the castle since 2006.

The complex is roughly 146 metres across, so it is too big to fit into one frame from close up. It works best if you pick one idea per photo: a long stretch of wall, a doorway or window set into the stone, or a wider view that shows how the buildings sit together. Because it lies just south of Nidaros Cathedral, you can also try a second shot that places the two together. Stand back a little and keep the vertical lines straight, using your phone's gridlines. Walk around a little before you settle on a view, as the shape of the buildings changes a lot from one side to the next.
text.geographic_location: The Archbishop's Palace is in Trondheim, just south of Nidaros Cathedral.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops listed nearby, so walk to Nidaros Cathedral and continue to its south side, where the palace lies. The phone icon on the map is about 20 m south-west of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the long stone walls and the sense of scale. Use the default lens (1x) for a natural-looking view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as stonework, windows and doorways.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 20 m south-west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line them up with the walls so the buildings do not lean. Choose one subject per shot, either a wide view of the long wall or a close detail of masonry. For variety, step back and include the cathedral just to the north as a second photo.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright so the sky is not washed out and the walls keep their colour. With the ultra-wide, keep the phone level to avoid stretched edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft light on an overcast day, or earlier or later in the day, usually suits stone walls better than harsh midday sun. Visit when it is quieter if you want clear views without people.

text.access_note: Parts of the complex are museums and used by the Church of Norway, so access may vary: check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft light or early/late light usually suits stone walls better than harsh midday sun.
The palace is quieter at some times of day than others.
The palace can be walked around and looks different from different sides.

name: Old Town Bridge
label: Old Town Bridge
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/342168270: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Gamle Bybro' (99 m across).
notes: Red wooden bridge with the 'Gate of Happiness' and views of the colourful riverside.

text.description: Gamle Bybro, the Old Town Bridge, carries you over the Nidelva river from the foot of Kjøpmannsgata to the Bakklandet neighbourhood. It is one of Trondheim's best-known landmarks, and it photographs well because the bridge, the water and the old buildings along the banks all fit into one calm scene. The bridge was designed by Johan Caspar von Cicignon as part of the rebuilding of Trondheim after the great fire of 1681 and was finished in 1685. It was first built of wood on three stone piers, with an iron gate in the middle that served as a guarded city gate until 1816. The access house at the west end still stands, while the one at the east end was taken down in 1824. The bridge was rebuilt in 1861 by the engineer Carl Adolf Dahl. Locals also call it Lykkens portal, the Gate of Happiness, after the waltz lyrics about the Nidelva by Kristian Oskar Hoddø. For a phone photo, aim to show the full length of the bridge with some river in front, rather than a tight close-up. Look for the rhythm of the railings and the reflections on the water, and leave a little space round the edges so you can crop later. Take a second shot along the bridge itself, which gives a feeling of walking across.
text.geographic_location: Where Kjøpmannsgata meets the Nidelva river. The bridge links the south end of Kjøpmannsgata with the Bakklandet neighbourhood across the Nidelva river.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stop is listed for this spot, so start from the foot of Kjøpmannsgata. Walk east from there to step onto the bridge. The phone icon on the map is about 20 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the bridge as you see it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the river and the buildings on the banks, and keep the bridge level near the centre so the edges do not stretch. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it for details such as the railings or the houses on the far bank.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 20 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the bridge up with a horizontal grid line so it looks straight. Keep a strip of water in the foreground and the far bank behind the bridge for depth. Try one shot in portrait orientation with more sky and reflection, and one in landscape orientation to show the full length of the bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bridge to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the sky keeps its colour and the bridge is not too dark. A Live Photo can catch gentle movement on the water, and night mode helps after dark if you hold the phone steady against a railing or wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or the hour before sunset usually gives softer light and calmer water. After dark, night mode can work well if there is lighting along the river.

text.access_note: The bridge is a public crossing between Kjøpmannsgata and Bakklandet, but check the official site before you go in case of works or closures.

name: Kristiansten Fortress
label: Kristiansten Fortress
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/10243780: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Kristiansten festning' (211 m across).
notes: 17th-century hilltop fortress with a fine view over the city.

text.description:
Kristiansten Fortress stands on a hill east of Trondheim city centre and was built to protect Trondheim from attack from the east. It was built after the great city fire of 1681. Work was finished in 1685, and the fortress did its job in 1718, when Swedish forces besieged the city and then withdrew. It was decommissioned in 1816. The centrepiece is the defensive tower, the Donjon, which has been a museum since 1997.

For a phone photo, the appeal is the mix of grass-topped ramparts, the pale tower and the open view over the city. The fortress also gives one of the best views of the 'strandlinja', a line along the hills of Bymarka that was once a shoreline of beaches and sea cliffs. It is seen best looking towards Byåsen. The grounds are fairly open, so you can walk round and try the tower from several sides. Use the walls and slopes as leading lines. If you want the tower and the sky together, step back along the grass rather than zooming in from close by. Keep an eye on your footing near the edges of the ramparts.
text.geographic_location: Kristiansten Fortress stands on a hill east of Trondheim city centre, overlooking the city and the area between Ila and Lade.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from Trondheim city centre and head east towards the hill where the fortress stands. The phone icon on the map is about 30 m north-west of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the tower and ramparts together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for long wall lines, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the hills towards Byåsen.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 30 m north-west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the tower on one of the vertical lines, with a wall or slope leading towards it. Keep the horizon level. For the view, turn towards Byåsen and use the zoom to show the line of the hills above the city.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or the tower to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the stonework does not wash out. Use panorama, moving slowly, for the sweep over the city.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a dry, clear day for the most distant view of the hills. Low sun early or late in the day gives the tower and walls more shape.

text.access_note: The grounds and the Donjon museum may have separate access arrangements, so check the official site before you go.

name: Bakklandet
label: Bakklandet
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/177561372: the OpenStreetMap point 'Bakklandet'.
notes: Cobbled lanes of pastel wooden houses and cafés.

text.description:
Bakklandet is a neighbourhood on the east bank of the Nidelva river in Trondheim, running between the Bakke Bridge (Bakke bru) and the Old Town Bridge (Gamle Bybro). It is made up of small wooden houses and narrow streets, and it counts among the city's major tourist attractions. That mix of low buildings, tight lanes and the river alongside is what makes it so easy to photograph: you get rows of houses, street scenes and water views within a short walk.

The area has a story worth knowing. In 1965 a road plan proposed demolishing a large part of Bakklandet for a four-lane motorway. Local people opposed it, and by the early 1980s the plan had been shelved.

For phone photos, think in small scenes rather than one big view. Look down a lane and let the street lead the eye towards the houses, or pick out a single doorway, window or wall. Walk a little and look back, because the same street often looks quite different from the other end. Switch on the gridlines to keep the vertical lines of the houses straight, and keep your phone level so the buildings don't lean. The streets are narrow, so step aside when others pass and keep your phone close to you.
text.geographic_location: Bakklandet is in the Østbyen borough of Trondheim, on the east side of the Nidelva river. It sits between the Bakke Bridge and the Old Town Bridge.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot, so head for the Old Town Bridge (Gamle Bybro) on the Nidelva river, which marks one end of Bakklandet, and start from there. The phone icon on the map is about 45 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for narrow streets, so you can fit in the houses on both sides. Use the default lens (1x) for most street scenes. If your phone has telephoto (2x-5x), use it for details such as doors, windows and wooden walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 45 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the houses with the vertical lines so they look straight. Use the street as a leading line towards the buildings. Take one wide shot, then move closer for a detail shot, such as a doorway or a wooden facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest or most important part of the scene to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky or the wall looks washed out. In shaded lanes, hold the phone steady and let night mode work if it switches on by itself.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or later in the day is likely to be quieter and the light softer in the narrow streets. Daytime is fine too, but expect more people in your shots.

text.access_note: Bakklandet is a neighbourhood of public streets where people live, so be considerate of residents.

name: Stiftsgården
label: Stiftsgården
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Stiftsgårdsparken' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Stiftsgårdsparken' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/87313159: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Stiftsgården' (87 m across).
notes: Large yellow 18th-century wooden palace, a royal residence.

text.description: Stiftsgården is the royal residence in Trondheim, a long, pale wooden palace on Munkegata, the city's main thoroughfare. It was built between 1774 and 1778 for Cecilie Christine Schøller, a wealthy merchant's widow, and has been used by royalty and their guests since 1800. With about 140 rooms and 4000 m², it is probably the largest wooden palace in Northern Europe, so it is more impressive for its size than for any fancy detail. It is built in the Baroque style, with touches of Rococo and neoclassicism. The best phone picture is from the garden side. That side has the old dormer windows, which stayed in place after some on other sides were removed following a small fire in 1841. The garden in front of you gives the building a green foreground, and the wide lawn and shady trees help the long façade sit neatly in the frame. Much of the garden was opened as a public park in 1906, and it is a peaceful spot with a fountain. Stand back far enough to get the whole width of the building, switch on the gridlines to keep the roofline level, and wait for a gap in the walkers if you want a clean shot. If you have time, the front of the palace on Munkegata makes a second photo, framed by Prydhagen and the statue of King Olav V. Only the outside is open for photography here, as interior photography is not permitted.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Trondheim, on Munkegata, the city's main street.
text.directions_text: No tram or train stop is listed for this spot, so start from the city centre of Trondheim and head for Munkegata, where the palace stands. Walk round to the garden side behind the building and into Stiftsgårdsparken. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole long façade from the garden. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a tidier, less stretched view of part of the building, and use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the dormer windows and roofline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Stiftsgårdsparken (behind the palace). The palace from its garden side, with the Rococo garden in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Keep the phone level using gridlines and put the lawn or flowerbeds in the lower part of the frame, with the palace across the middle. Take one wide shot of the whole palace and one closer shot of the dormer windows. For a different angle, Prydhagen on the Munkegata side shows the main façade with the statue of King Olav V.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the palace to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the pale walls keep their detail. Take a few frames, as people often walk through the garden.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Try the morning or a bright but slightly overcast day, when the garden side is evenly lit and the colours are soft.

text.access_note: The garden is a free public park, but check the official site before you go for any palace opening, tours or garden closures; interior photography is not permitted.

name: Rockheim
label: Rockheim
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Brattørkaia' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Brattørkaia nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/104018578: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Rockheim' (82 m across).
notes: Striking national museum of pop and rock on the waterfront.

text.description:
Rockheim is Norway's national museum of popular music, covering the 1950s to today. It sits in a grain warehouse built in 1919, and it opened in 2010. The old building now carries a glass-clad box on top that juts out over the edge. The glass is printed with reproductions of album covers and lit from behind by 13,000 individually controllable LEDs. Visitors can even change the colours using their phones. That mix of plain old warehouse and colourful modern box is what makes it good to photograph.

The best phone picture is a street-level view from the opposite side of the road, looking across at the whole building. It works best after dark, when the lit box glows against the darker warehouse below. Stay on the pavement and keep clear of traffic and any entrances while you take your photo.

If you want a closer view of the glowing top box, walk a little nearer and shoot upwards. Check the pavement and your surroundings before you step back to fit more in. Daytime pictures also work if you want to show the old warehouse walls, though the lights are much less obvious.
text.geographic_location: Rockheim stands on Brattørkaia in Trondheim, in the old grain warehouse that now houses the museum. The street in front of it is the best place to photograph it from.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stops are listed for this spot, so head to Brattørkaia, for example on foot from central Trondheim. Once there, walk to the opposite side of the street from the museum. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from across the street. If the building does not fit, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x). Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out the glowing box at the top.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Brattørkaia (opposite side of the street from the museum, looking across at the building). A night view of the illuminated museum across the road, taken from a hotel-side vantage point. From there you look across the road at the whole building, with the museum to the south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the walls of the old warehouse straight against them. Put the glass box in the upper part of the frame and leave the lower part for the warehouse. For a different angle, walk closer to the entrance and shoot upwards to show the lit box on its own.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: After dark, use night mode and brace your phone against a post or your own body to keep it steady. Tap on the lit box to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the LED colours stay rich and do not wash out to white.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: At night, when the lights on the glass box are on.

text.access_note: The building can be photographed from the public street. If you plan to go inside the museum, check the official Rockheim site for visitor information before you go.

name: Trampe Bicycle Lift
label: Trampe Bicycle Lift
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/4428040701: the OpenStreetMap point 'Trampe bicycle lift'.
notes: The world's first bicycle lift, next to the Bakklandet hill.

text.description: Trampe is a bicycle lift in Trondheim. It was invented and installed in 1993 by Jarle Wanwik, and in 2013 it was upgraded and rebranded as CycloCable by Skirail, part of the Poma group. A cyclist puts their right foot on the starting point, keeps the left foot on the pedal, presses the start button and is pushed uphill by a footplate that emerges. The lift is free to use. It photographs well because the action is easy to read: a rider glides up the slope with one leg stretched out, and a few frames later they have gone. It is used a lot in summer, by commuters and tourists alike, so you can usually wait for a rider to come along. First-timers often forget to keep the right leg outstretched and the body tilted forward, which makes balance hard. That can make for a lively picture, but be kind and don't film anyone who is struggling. Keep clear of the lift track so you don't get in anyone's way. For the best photo, wait until a rider is partway up the slope, then take a few quick frames. Take one wider shot that shows the setting and one closer shot of the rider's pose. Check the official site before you go if you want to be sure the lift is running.
text.geographic_location: Trampe is a bicycle lift in Trondheim, Norway.
text.directions_text: There are no nearby stops listed for this spot, so head to the lift from central Trondheim on foot or by bike, using the map. Walk west from it and the lift comes into view. The phone icon on the map is about 80 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) from where you stand, to bring the rider and slope closer. Then use the default lens (1x) once you are nearer, to show the setting around the lift.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 80 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. From there you can see the rider and the slope without crowding the track.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the rider on one of the third lines, leaving space ahead of them in the direction they are moving. Take one frame with the whole slope and surroundings, then zoom in for a closer shot of the outstretched leg. Stay well clear of the track and don't step into the rider's path.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the rider to lock focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the rider doesn't turn into a silhouette. Live Photos or motion mode can catch the movement, and you can pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Summer is when the lift is used most, so you are more likely to see riders then. Check the official site before you go to confirm that it is running.

text.access_note: The lift is free to use, but check the official site before you go to confirm that it is running.
claims_not_in_sources: Waiting near the lift in summer will usually give a chance of seeing a rider using it.
Bright sky behind a rider can make them appear as a silhouette unless exposure is lowered.

name: Ravnkloa
label: Ravnkloa
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ravnkloa' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM R14182258 (Ravnkloa): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Harbour at the end of Munkegata, departure point for boats to Munkholmen.

text.description:
Ravnkloa is the square at the lower end of Munkegata, beside the fish market, and it is a handy place for a quick, varied photo stop. Three things share the space: the fish market buildings, a copy of the old Ravnkloa clock, and the sculpture "The Last of the Vikings" by Nils Aas. Together they give you a good sense of the harbour-side setting without having to walk far.

The square works well because you can take several different pictures from almost the same spot. Start with a wide view that has the fish market buildings and the clock copy in the same frame. Then turn to the sculpture for a closer, simpler shot. The clock makes a clear focal point, and the market buildings behind it show where you are.

If you want a second view, go to the canal quay at Ravnkloa. Looking north from there, you can photograph the harbour and the boat departures towards Munkholmen along the water. That is a different picture from the square, so it is worth taking both.

The square is a place where people walk through and stop, so wait a moment for a gap if you want a cleaner frame. Keep your phone lens clean, as harbour air can leave a film on it. Boats toward Munkholmen leave from the canal quay.
text.geographic_location: Ravnkloa is in central Trondheim, at the bottom end of Munkegata beside the fish market and the harbour canal.
text.directions_text: Start from the city centre and walk to the lower, harbour end of Munkegata, where the square lies beside the fish market. The phone icon on the map is on the square itself. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the square as a whole, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the fish market buildings and the clock copy will not fit, and try telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the sculpture.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you can see the fish market buildings and the square with the copy of the old Ravnkloa clock, with "The Last of the Vikings" as a second subject.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and use them to keep the market buildings upright. Put the clock copy on one of the grid lines and let the buildings fill the background. Then move closer to the sculpture for a simple second photo. For a different view, go to the canal quay and shoot north towards the harbour and the Munkholmen boat departures.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the clock or sculpture to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright and the subject looks dark. Use portrait mode on the sculpture if you want the background softened.

text.access_note: The square is free to visit; no ticket is needed for the photo spot.

name: Church of Our Lady
label: Vår Frue Church
camera_source: Commons cluster (8 photos), weak. Moved 28 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 50 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/89340594: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Vår Frue kirke' (69 m across).
notes: Historic stone church in the city centre.

text.description: Our Lady's Church (Vår Frue kirke) is a grey stone medieval church in the middle of Trondheim, a few blocks north of Nidaros Cathedral. It is a good photo stop because the bare stone walls, the tall tower with its pyramid-shaped roof and spire, and the long body of the church all fit into one calm, simple picture. It makes a good second subject after the cathedral. The church was built in the late 1100s and mixes Romanesque and Gothic styles. It has been through several fires and rebuilds, including the great city fire of 1651, when only the walls were left standing. The tower you see today at the west end dates from the 1700s, and the spire was added in 1779. In the 1950s the whitewash was taken off the outside, so the stone looks much as it would have done in the Middle Ages. The church is about 64 metres long, so it is hard to fit in from close by. Step back where you can, or use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) and keep the phone level so the walls do not lean. Use the default lens (1x) for the whole building and the telephoto lens for details such as the spire or the stonework. Keep an eye out for people, cars and signs at street level, and move a few steps to tidy the frame.
text.geographic_location: In the Midtbyen (downtown) area of Trondheim, a few blocks north of Nidaros Cathedral.
text.directions_text: Head for the Midtbyen area, a few blocks north of Nidaros Cathedral, and walk north from the cathedral to reach the church. From the phone icon on the map, the church is about 1 minute on foot to the south-east. The phone icon on the map is about 50 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the long church in from close up, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the tower, spire and stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 50 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. It is about 1 minute on foot from there to the church itself.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical grid line so it stands straight. Keep the phone level, and hold it at chest height rather than tilting it up, to limit leaning walls. For a second picture, move in and use telephoto to fill the frame with the stonework and spire.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the pale sky does not wash out the grey stone. Use portrait mode only if a person is standing in front of the church.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light brings out the texture of the stonework. On grey days the stone looks even and moody; in the evening, switch on night mode and rest your elbows against something steady.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the street; if you want to go inside, check the official site before you go for visiting times and any restrictions, and dress respectfully as it is a working church.
claims_not_in_sources: From the north-west, the west tower and the long north side of the church are the main things visible.
Soft morning or late-afternoon light suits stonework and gives more texture.
The outside can be seen from the street and the church may have visiting times or restrictions inside.
Walking north from Nidaros Cathedral leads towards the church.

name: Trondheim Torget and Olav Tryggvason Statue
label: Torget Square
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Torvet' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Torvet' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/78348: the OpenStreetMap point 'Olav Tryggvason'.
notes: Main square with the tall column statue of the Viking king who founded the city.

text.description:
Torvet, Trondheim's main square, is the easy one on this map: the subject stands right in the middle of it. The Olav Tryggvason monument is a tall obelisk topped with a statue of the king who founded the city. It stands where the two main streets, Munkegata and Kongens gate, cross. The statue is 18 metres high and was made by the sculptor Wilhelm Rasmussen. It was unveiled in 1921. Around its base, a cobblestone mosaic from 1930 forms a huge sundial. It is set to UTC+1, so in summer it reads an hour out. A water feature was added to the base in 2020, which gives you a second, lower detail to photograph.

The column works because it is a clear vertical shape with open space around it, so it is simple to frame. The roof of Vår Frue church can show behind the monument, so try lining the two up. For a closer shot, the base, the sundial pattern and the water feature make a good foreground. Take a few steps around the column to change what sits behind the king. Check the square for temporary market or Christmas-market stalls, which can appear and change what you can see.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Trondheim, on the main city square, Torvet, where Munkegata crosses Kongens gate.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stop is listed for this spot, so start from the centre of Trondheim and head for Torvet, the main square at the crossing of Munkegata and Kongens gate. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole monument. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the column and the sundial mosaic together, and telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the statue's figure at the top.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Torvet (on the square itself, close to the statue at its centre). The Olav Tryggvason monument rising from the middle of the square, with the roof of Vår Frue church visible behind it in one published photo.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the column up with a vertical line so it does not lean. Hold the phone low and tilt up only a little, or the column will taper. For a second picture, move in and frame the water feature and the sundial mosaic at the base.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the top of the statue to set focus and exposure, then pull the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the stone stays dark enough to show detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Try a quieter time of day, when the sun is out, so the stone and the sundial pattern show up clearly.

text.access_note: Torvet is an open public square; check the official site before you go if market or event stalls are planned.
